“What a number of bond robberies there have been lately!” I observed
one morning, laying aside the newspaper. “Poirot, let us forsake
the science of detection, and take to crime instead!”

“You are on the—how do you say it?—get-rich-quick tack, eh, _mon
ami_?”

“Well, look at this last _coup_, the million dollars’ worth of
Liberty Bonds which the London and Scottish Bank were sending to
New York, and which disappeared in such a remarkable manner on
board the _Olympia_.”

“If it were not for the _mal de mer_, and the difficulty of
practising the so excellent method of Laverguier for a longer time
than the few hours of crossing the channel, I should delight to
voyage myself on one of these big liners,” murmured Poirot dreamily.

“Yes, indeed,” I said enthusiastically. “Some of them must be
perfect palaces; the swimming-baths, the lounges, the restaurant,
the palm courts—really, it must be hard to believe that one is on
the sea.”

“Me, I always know when I am on the sea,” said Poirot sadly. “And
all those bagatelles that you enumerate, they say nothing to me;
but, my friend, consider for a moment the geniuses that travel as
it were incognito! On board these floating palaces, as you so
justly call them, one would meet the élite, the _haute noblesse_
of the criminal world!”

I laughed.

“So that’s the way your enthusiasm runs! You would have liked to
cross swords with the man who sneaked the Liberty Bonds?”

The landlady interrupted us.

“A young lady as wants to see you, Mr. Poirot. Here’s her card.”

The card bore the inscription: Miss Esmée Farquhar, and Poirot,
after diving under the table to retrieve a stray crumb, and putting
it carefully in the waste-paper-basket, nodded to the landlady to
admit her.

In another minute one of the most charming girls I have ever seen
was ushered into the room. She was perhaps about five-and-twenty,
with big brown eyes and a perfect figure. She was well-dressed and
perfectly composed in manner.

“Sit down, I beg of you, mademoiselle. This is my friend, Captain
Hastings, who aids me in my little problems.”

“I am afraid it is a big problem I have brought you to-day, Monsieur
Poirot,” said the girl, giving me a pleasant bow as she seated
herself. “I dare say you have read about it in the papers. I am
referring to the theft of Liberty Bonds on the _Olympia_.” Some
astonishment must have shown itself in Poirot’s face, for she
continued quickly: “You are doubtless asking yourself what I have
to do with a grave institution like the London and Scottish Bank.
In one sense nothing, in another sense everything. You see, Monsieur
Poirot, I am engaged to Mr. Philip Ridgeway.”

“Aha! and Mr. Philip Ridgeway——”

“Was in charge of the bonds when they were stolen. Of course no
actual blame can attach to him, it was not his fault in any way.
Nevertheless, he is half distraught over the matter, and his uncle,
I know, insists that he must carelessly have mentioned having them
in his possession. It is a terrible set-back in his career.”

“Who is his uncle?”

“Mr. Vavasour, joint general manager of the London and Scottish
Bank.”

“Suppose, Miss Farquhar, that you recount to me the whole story?”

“Very well. As you know, the Bank wished to extend their credits
in America, and for this purpose decided to send over a million
dollars in Liberty Bonds. Mr. Vavasour selected his nephew, who
had occupied a position of trust in the Bank for many years and
who was conversant with all the details of the Bank’s dealings in
New York, to make the trip. The Olympia sailed from Liverpool on
the 23rd, and the bonds were handed over to Philip on the morning
of that day by Mr. Vavasour and Mr. Shaw, the two joint general
managers of the London and Scottish Bank. They were counted,
enclosed in a package, and sealed in his presence, and he then
locked the package at once in his portmanteau.”

“A portmanteau with an ordinary lock?”

“No, Mr. Shaw insisted on a special lock being fitted to it by
Hubbs’s. Philip, as I say, placed the package at the bottom of the
trunk. It was stolen just a few hours before reaching New York. A
rigorous search of the whole ship was made, but without result.
The bonds seemed literally to have vanished into thin air.”

Poirot made a grimace.

“But they did not vanish absolutely, since I gather that they were
sold in small parcels within half an hour of the docking of the
_Olympia_! Well, undoubtedly the next thing is for me to see Mr.
Ridgeway.”

“I was about to suggest that you should lunch with me at the
‘Cheshire Cheese.’ Philip will be there. He is meeting me, but does
not yet know that I have been consulting you on his behalf.”

We agreed to this suggestion readily enough, and drove there in a
taxi.

Mr. Philip Ridgeway was there before us, and looked somewhat
surprised to see his fiancée arriving with two complete strangers.
He was a nice-looking young fellow, tall and spruce, with a touch
of greying hair at the temples, though he could not have been much
over thirty.

Miss Farquhar went up to him and laid her hand on his arm.

“You must forgive my acting without consulting you, Philip,” she
said. “Let me introduce you to Monsieur Hercule Poirot, of whom
you must often have heard, and his friend, Captain Hastings.”

Ridgeway looked very astonished.

“Of course I have heard of you, Monsieur Poirot,” he said, as he
shook hands. “But I had no idea that Esmée was thinking of
consulting you about my—our trouble.”

“I was afraid you would not let me do it, Philip,” said Miss
Farquhar meekly.

“So you took care to be on the safe side,” he observed, with a
smile. “I hope Monsieur Poirot will be able to throw some light on
this extraordinary puzzle, for I confess frankly that I am nearly
out of my mind with worry and anxiety about it.”

Indeed, his face looked drawn and haggard and showed only too
clearly the strain under which he was labouring.

“Well, well,” said Poirot. “Let us lunch, and over lunch we will
put our heads together and see what can be done. I want to hear
Mr. Ridgeway’s story from his own lips.”

Whilst we discussed the excellent steak and kidney pudding of the
establishment, Philip Ridgeway narrated the circumstances leading
to the disappearance of the bonds. His story agreed with that of
Miss Farquhar in every particular. When he had finished, Poirot
took up the thread with a question.

“What exactly led you to discover that the bonds had been stolen,
Mr. Ridgeway?”

He laughed rather bitterly.

“The thing stared me in the face, Monsieur Poirot. I couldn’t have
missed it. My cabin trunk was half out from under the bunk and all
scratched and cut about where they’d tried to force the lock.”

“But I understood that it had been opened with a key?”

“That’s so. They tried to force it, but couldn’t. And, in the end,
they must have got it unlocked somehow or other.”

“Curious,” said Poirot, his eyes beginning to flicker with the
green light I knew so well. “Very curious! They waste much, much
time trying to prise it open, and then—_sapristi!_ they find that
they have the key all the time—for each of Hubbs’s locks are
unique.”

“That’s just why they couldn’t have had the key. It never left me
day or night.”

“You are sure of that?”

“I can swear to it, and besides, if they had had the key or a
duplicate, why should they waste time trying to force an obviously
unforceable lock?”

“Ah! there is exactly the question we are asking ourselves! I
venture to prophesy that the solution, if we ever find it, will
hinge on that curious fact. I beg of you not to assault me if I
ask you one more question: _Are you perfectly certain you did not
leave the trunk unlocked?_”

Philip Ridgeway merely looked at him, and Poirot gesticulated
apologetically.

“Ah, but these things can happen, I assure you! Very well, the
bonds were stolen from the trunk. What did the thief do with them?
How did he manage to get ashore with them?”

“Ah!” cried Ridgeway. “That’s just it. How? Word was passed to the
Customs authorities, and every soul that left the ship was gone
over with a toothcomb!”

“And the bonds, I gather, made a bulky package?”

“Certainly they did. They could hardly have been hidden on board—and
anyway we know they weren’t because they were offered for sale
within half an hour of the _Olympia’s_ arrival, long before I got
the cables going and the numbers sent out. One broker swears he
bought some of them even before the _Olympia_ got in. But you can’t
send bonds by wireless.”

“Not by wireless, but did any tug come alongside?”

“Only the official ones, and that was after the alarm was given
when every one was on the look-out. I was watching out myself for
their being passed over to some one that way. My God, Monsieur
Poirot, this thing will drive me mad! People are beginning to say
I stole them myself.”

“But you also were searched on landing, weren’t you?” asked Poirot
gently.

“Yes.”

The young man stared at him in a puzzled manner.

“You do not catch my meaning, I see,” said Poirot, smiling
enigmatically. “Now I should like to make a few inquiries at the
Bank.”

Ridgeway produced a card and scribbled a few words on it.

“Send this in and my uncle will see you at once.”

Poirot thanked him, bade farewell to Miss Farquhar, and together
we started out for Threadneedle Street and the head office of the
London and Scottish Bank. On production of Ridgeway’s card, we were
led through the labyrinth of counters and desks, skirting paying-in
clerks and paying-out clerks and up to a small office on the first
floor where the joint general managers received us. They were two
grave gentlemen, who had grown grey in the service of the Bank.
Mr. Vavasour had a short white beard, Mr. Shaw was clean shaven.

“I understand you are strictly a private inquiry agent?” said Mr.
Vavasour. “Quite so, quite so. We have, of course, placed ourselves
in the hands of Scotland Yard. Inspector McNeil has charge of the
case. A very able officer, I believe.”

“I am sure of it,” said Poirot politely. “You will permit a few
questions, on your nephew’s behalf? About this lock, who ordered
it from Hubbs’s?”

“I ordered it myself,” said Mr. Shaw. “I would not trust to any
clerk in the matter. As to the keys, Mr. Ridgeway had one, and the
other two are held by my colleague and myself.”

“And no clerk has had access to them?”

Mr. Shaw turned inquiringly to Mr. Vavasour. “I think I am correct
in saying that they have remained in the safe where we placed them
on the 23rd,” said Mr. Vavasour. “My colleague was unfortunately
taken ill a fortnight ago—in fact on the very day that Philip left
us. He has only just recovered.”

“Severe bronchitis is no joke to a man of my age,” said Mr. Shaw
ruefully. “But I am afraid Mr. Vavasour has suffered from the hard
work entailed by my absence, especially with this unexpected worry
coming on top of everything.”

Poirot asked a few more questions. I judged that he was endeavouring
to gauge the exact amount of intimacy between uncle and nephew.
Mr. Vavasour’s answers were brief and punctilious. His nephew was
a trusted official of the Bank, and had no debts or money
difficulties that he knew of. He had been entrusted with similar
missions in the past. Finally we were politely bowed out.

“I am disappointed,” said Poirot, as we emerged into the street.

“You hoped to discover more? They are such stodgy old men.”

“It is not their stodginess which disappoints me, _mon ami_. I do
not expect to find in a Bank manager a ‘keen financier with an
eagle glance’ as your favourite works of fiction put it. No, I am
disappointed in the case—it is too easy!”

“Easy?”

“Yes, do you not find it almost childishly simple?”

“You know who stole the bonds?”

“I do.”

“But then—we must—why——”

“Do not confuse and fluster yourself, Hastings. We are not going
to do anything at present.”

“But why? What are you waiting for?”

“For the _Olympia_. She is due on her return trip from New York on
Tuesday.”

“But if you know who stole the bonds, why wait? He may escape.”

“To a South Sea island where there is no extradition? No, _mon
ami_, he would find life very uncongenial there. As to why I
wait—_eh bien_ to the intelligence of Hercule Poirot the case is
perfectly clear, but for the benefit of others, not so greatly
gifted by the good God—the Inspector McNeil, for instance—it would
be as well to make a few inquiries to establish the facts. One must
have consideration for those less gifted than oneself.”

“Good Lord, Poirot! Do you know, I’d give a considerable sum of
money to see you make a thorough ass of yourself—just for once.
You’re so confoundedly conceited!”

“Do not enrage yourself, Hastings. In verity, I observe that there
are times when you almost detest me! Alas, I suffer the penalties
of greatness!”

The little man puffed out his chest, and sighed so comically that
I was forced to laugh.

Tuesday saw us speeding to Liverpool in a first-class carriage of
the L. & N.W.R. Poirot had obstinately refused to enlighten me as
to his suspicions—or certainties. He contented himself with
expressing surprise that I, too, was not equally _au fait_ with
the situation. I disdained to argue, and entrenched my curiosity
behind a rampart of pretended indifference.

Once arrived at the quay alongside which lay the big transatlantic
liner, Poirot became brisk and alert. Our proceedings consisted in
interviewing four successive stewards and inquiring after a friend
of Poirot’s who had crossed to New York on the 23rd.

“An elderly gentleman, wearing glasses. A great invalid, hardly
moved out of his cabin.”

The description appeared to tally with one Mr. Ventnor who had
occupied the cabin C 24 which was next to that of Philip Ridgeway.
Although unable to see how Poirot had deduced Mr. Ventnor’s
existence and personal appearance, I was keenly excited.

“Tell me,” I cried, “was this gentleman one of the first to land
when you got to New York?” The steward shook his head.

“No, indeed, sir, he was one of the last off the boat.”

I retired crestfallen, and observed Poirot grinning at me. He
thanked the steward, a note changed hands, and we took our
departure.

“It’s all very well,” I remarked heatedly, “but that last answer
must have damped your precious theory, grin as you please!”

“As usual, you see nothing, Hastings. That last answer is, on the
contrary, the coping-stone of my theory.”

I flung up my hands in despair.

“I give it up.”

When we were in the train, speeding towards London, Poirot wrote
busily for a few minutes, sealing up the result in an envelope.

“This is for the good Inspector McNeil. We will leave it at Scotland
Yard in passing, and then to the Rendezvous Restaurant, where I
have asked Miss Esmée Farquhar to do us the honour of dining with
us.”

“What about Ridgeway?”

“What about him?” asked Poirot with a twinkle.

“Why, you surely don’t think—you can’t——”

“The habit of incoherence is growing upon you, Hastings. As a
matter of fact I _did_ think. If Ridgeway had been the thief—which
was perfectly possible—the case would have been charming; a piece
of neat methodical work.”

“But not so charming for Miss Farquhar.”

“Possibly you are right. Therefore all is for the best. Now,
Hastings, let us review the case. I can see that you are dying to
do so. The sealed package is removed from the trunk and vanishes,
as Miss Farquhar puts it, into thin air. We will dismiss the thin
air theory, which is not practicable at the present stage of
science, and consider what is likely to have become of it. Every
one asserts the incredibility of its being smuggled ashore——”

“Yes, but we know——”

“_You_ may know, Hastings. I do not. I take the view that, since
it seemed incredible, it _was_ incredible. Two possibilities
remain: it was hidden on board—also rather difficult—or it was
thrown overboard.”

“With a cork on it, do you mean?”

“Without a cork.”

I stared.

“But if the bonds were thrown overboard, they couldn’t have been
sold in New York.”

“I admire your logical mind, Hastings. The bonds were sold in New
York, therefore they were not thrown overboard. You see where that
leads us?”

“Where we were when we started.”

“_Jamais de la vie!_ If the package was thrown overboard, and the
bonds were sold in New York, the package could not have contained
the bonds. Is there any evidence that the package _did_ contain
the bonds? Remember, Mr. Ridgeway never opened it from the time it
was placed in his hands in London.”

“Yes, but then——”

Poirot waved an impatient hand.

“Permit me to continue. The last moment that the bonds are seen as
bonds is in the office of the London and Scottish Bank on the
morning of the 23rd. They reappear in New York half an hour after
the _Olympia_ gets in, and according to one man, whom nobody
listens to, actually _before_ she gets in. Supposing then, that
they have never been on the _Olympia_ at all? Is there any other
way they could get to New York? Yes. The _Gigantic_ leaves
Southampton on the same day as the _Olympia_, and she holds the
record for the Atlantic. Mailed by the _Gigantic_, the bonds would
be in New York the day before the _Olympia_ arrived. All is clear,
the case begins to explain itself. The sealed packet is only a
dummy, and the moment of its substitution must be in the office in
the Bank. It would be an easy matter for any of the three men
present to have prepared a duplicate package which could be
substituted for the genuine one. _Très bien_, the bonds are mailed
to a confederate in New York, with instructions to sell as soon as
the _Olympia_ is in, but some one must travel on the _Olympia_ to
engineer the supposed moment of the robbery.”

“But why?”

“Because if Ridgeway merely opens the packet and finds it a dummy,
suspicion flies at once to London. No, the man on board in the
cabin next door does his work, pretends to force the lock in an
obvious manner so as to draw immediate attention to the theft,
really unlocks the trunk with a duplicate key, throws the package
overboard and waits until the last to leave the boat. Naturally he
wears glasses to conceal his eyes, and is an invalid since he does
not want to run the risk of meeting Ridgeway. He steps ashore in
New York and returns by the first boat available.”

“But who—which was he?”

“The man who had a duplicate key, the man who ordered the lock,
the man who has _not_ been severely ill with bronchitis at his home
in the country—_enfin_, that ‘stodgy’ old man, Mr. Shaw! There are
criminals in high places sometimes, my friend. Ah, here we are.
Mademoiselle, I have succeeded! You permit?”

And, beaming, Poirot kissed the astonished girl lightly on either
cheek!

suspicious of everyone else.  There was a rather shady-looking

think he was merely an ordinary passenger.”

“And what about your fiancé?  What is his account of the matter?”
“Vanished into thin air? That is a curious phrase, mademoiselle.
It suggests, shall we say, a less materialistic method of theft
than the ordinary pickpocket or cracksman.  Tell me, was your fiancé
the only person who had access to this portmanteau?”
“Thin air, you say?  That is precisely what makes the case so
interesting, _mademoiselle_.  Vanishing into thin air is not usually
the method employed by the common thief.  It suggests a certain
amount of ingenuity, even of… artistry.”
“The thin air, eh?  A most unsatisfactory element in which to
conduct a search.  And was this portmanteau, Mademoiselle, ever
out of Mr. Ridgeway’s possession from the moment he locked it until
the discovery of the theft?”
“The police, I understand, have made several arrests?”

“Yes, several stewards and other members of the crew were
detained, but nothing whatever could be proved against them.  Then
the suspicion fell on Philip, and it is that which has brought me
to you.  Mr. Vavasour is a very influential man, and the
investigation is being hushed up as much as possible, but—I believe
Philip is innocent.”  Miss Farquhar’s voice trembled slightly.

sold in small parcels within half an hour of the docking of the
_Olympia_! Well, undoubtedly the next thing is for me to see Mr.
Ridgeway.”

‘Cheshire Cheese.’ Philip will be there. He is meeting me, but does
not yet know that I have been consulting you on his behalf.”

We agreed to this suggestion readily enough, and drove there in a

Bonds.  A very responsible task, no?”

calm, was clearly nervous. He answered Poirot’s questions readily
enough, but with a certain guardedness in his manner.  He confirmed
the details of the journey, the handing over of the bonds, the
special lock on the portmanteau, and the subsequent discovery of
the theft.  He insisted repeatedly that he had not the slightest
idea how the theft had been committed.  His uncle, Mr. Vavasour, he

not been wasting my time.”

He leaned back, his eyes twinkling.  “The case, my dear Hastings,
was, as I said, too easy.  Too pat. Too convenient.”
“This,” he said, handing me the envelope, “is for Inspector
McNeil.  You will deliver it to him personally.  I think you will
find that it contains sufficient evidence to satisfy him.”  He
leaned back, a contented smile on his face.  “The case of the
stolen Liberty Bonds is closed.”
“This,” he announced, handing me the envelope, “is for Inspector
McNeil. You will see that the culprit is Mr. Shaw.”

“Mr. Shaw?” I exclaimed, utterly bewildered. “But why? What reason
had he?”

“The reason, my friend, is a very simple one, and I must confess
it appears to have eluded your penetration completely.” He chuckled
softly.  “Mr. Shaw was ill, you remember? Confined to his bed, as
his colleague was good enough to testify.   He had bronchitis.   And
so—he had an excellent excuse for not being on board, and did not
even need to leave the country.”

“That is for Inspector McNeil,” he explained. “It contains a short
account of the facts as I see them, with the name of the culprit.
It is not necessary to proceed further.”

“But who is the culprit?” I asked impatiently.

“Mr. Shaw, of course.”

“Shaw? But why?”

“Because it was he who was ill, and who therefore did not leave his
cabin during the whole voyage. Because he was in a position to
obtain a duplicate key of the special lock and place the bonds in
Mr. Ridgeway’s trunk. The bonds were transferred in the tugboat,
and the trick was so cleverly planned that the package of bonds
could pass as part of the ship’s stores, and no one would think of
suspecting that they were not.”

“This goes to Inspector McNeil,” he explained. “It contains a
summary of the facts, and a suggestion that he should immediately
arrest Mr. Shaw, the joint general manager of the London and
Scottish Bank.”

“Shaw? But why Shaw?”

“Because, _mon ami_, Mr. Shaw was ill with bronchitis from the
23rd to the day of the arrival of the _Olympia_ in New York. He
could not have been present in person to steal the bonds—yet, they
were stolen.”

“But—how?”

“Ah, that is what is interesting. Mr. Shaw was ill in his own
house. The keys to the special lock had not left the safe. Yet the
bonds were removed. It is clear, _n’est-ce pas_?”

“But I still don’t see how...”

“It is so simple! The bonds were not stolen on board the _Olympia_.
They were never there! This Mr. Ventnor was an excellent mimic, and
he was Mr. Shaw’s double. He received the package from Mr. Shaw,
transferred the contents into a dummy package, which was sealed up
with the same type of lock, and which the manager had prepared
beforehand, and then sailed over to New York with the substituted
package. That dummy package was in the trunk which was scratched and
prized open.”

“This is for the good Inspector McNeil. We will leave it at Scotland
Yard in passing, and then to the Rendezvous Restaurant, where I
have asked Miss Esmée Farquhar to do us the honour of dining with
us.”

“What about Ridgeway?”

“What about him?” asked Poirot with a twinkle.

“Why, you surely don’t think—you can’t——”

“My dear Hastings, you allow your imagination to run away with you!
I accuse no one. I merely wish to put a few finishing touches to
my little picture. As for Mr. Ridgeway, he is—ah—an innocent
party, most certainly, most certainly!”

I was about to ask a question, but Poirot stopped me with a raised
hand.

“Let me assure you that it is Mr. Shaw who is the guilty party.
He stole the bonds, and not only stole them but sold them within
half an hour of the docking of the _Olympia_!”

“But how?”

“That is what I am going to explain to you.”

“My dear Hastings, you are as dense as a London fog! Do you think I
would have troubled to come all the way to Liverpool to interview
stewards if I thought the matter so simple as all that?  The theft
of the bonds was a clever thing, very cleverly done.  But not
clever enough for Hercule Poirot!”
“My dear Hastings, you have a truly deplorable imagination. I do
not suspect Mr. Ridgeway of anything whatsoever. On the contrary, I
have every reason to believe that he is a most innocent young man,
the victim of a very cleverly conceived plot.”

“Then who—?”

“Patience, my friend. You will soon see.”

“My dear Hastings, you are too excitable! I think nothing of the
sort. I am merely going to show Miss Esmée Farquhar how easily
her fiancé might have been framed.”

“Framed?”

“Precisely. It is a very pretty little piece of work, and I am
delighted with my performance. Mr. Shaw, you see, was taken ill on
the day Philip sailed. A very convenient illness, I think you will
agree!”

“My dear Hastings, you are so slow! You have the mind of a
tortoise!  Of course I think that Mr. Philip Ridgeway is innocent
of the theft of the Liberty Bonds. The evidence points so strongly
to him, that it must inevitably be somebody else. The whole thing
is a cleverly devised scheme.”

“But who is the guilty party?”

“Ah, that is what we shall discover presently at the Rendezvous.”

“The habit of incoherence is growing upon you, Hastings. As a
matter of fact I _did_ think. If Ridgeway had been the thief—which
was perfectly possible—the case would have been charming; a piece
of neat methodical work.”

“But not so charming for Miss Farquhar.”

“Precisely.  And that is why I have decided it was not he.  A man
does not steal a million dollars’ worth of Liberty Bonds for the
sake of a charming girl, unless, of course, she is exceptionally
charming.  And Miss Farquhar—though charming—is not exceptional.
 Besides, his method was too clumsy.  The forced lock was a
dangerous blunder.  No, my friend, I think we shall find the thief
in a much more unexpected quarter.”

“Precisely.  And it is not charming for Mr. Shaw either.  For Mr.
Shaw, my friend, was the thief.”
“Precisely.  And yet, the young lady is charming, and in no way
connected with the theft.  It was—shall we say—a little too
convenient.  The theft, the forced lock, the immediate sale of the
bonds… it all pointed too neatly to Ridgeway.”
“Precisely! That is why I have eliminated him from my calculations.
The thief was far too clever to run the risk of endangering Miss
Farquhar’s happiness. No, the thief was—Mr. Shaw!”

“Shaw?” I gasped.  “But why? And how?”

“Because he was ill, and confined to his cabin. Because he had access
to the keys.  Because he could easily pass the bonds to a confederate
on a passing tug.”

“Precisely. And since it is not charming for Miss Farquhar, it is
not true.  My dear Hastings, you will learn in time that sentiment
plays an important part in crime. The criminal is, in the main, an
emotional creature. Now consider Mr. Shaw.  He was ill at the
precise moment when the theft took place.  A most fortunate illness,
was it not?”

“Possibly you are right. Therefore all is for the best. Now,
Hastings, let us review the case. I can see that you are dying to
do so. The sealed package is removed from the trunk and vanishes,
as Miss Farquhar puts it, into thin air. We will dismiss the thin
air theory, which is not practicable at the present stage of
science, and consider what is likely to have become of it. Every
one asserts the incredibility of its being smuggled ashore——”

“Yes, but we know——”

“We know nothing of the sort, Hastings, until we have proved it.
The bonds were sold almost immediately on arrival in New York.  That
means that the thief must have had a confederate on shore ready to
receive them.  A bulky package is difficult to secrete, but a
smaller parcel—— Now, the point of the Hubbs lock is that it is
unique.  Mr. Shaw had the key, as did Mr. Vavasour and Mr. Ridgeway.  All three keys remained in the Bank until the last moment, and Mr. Shaw was ill.  Mr. Vavasour, therefore, would have to have had access to his colleague's key.”

“We know nothing, Hastings, until we have proved it.  The point is,
that it was not smuggled ashore.  It was sent ashore by a perfectly
legitimate method—a method so obvious, that it has escaped the
notice of everyone.  The bonds were sent ashore in the luggage of
Mr. Shaw.”

“—that it _was_ smuggled ashore. But how? The answer is simple
enough. It was not smuggled ashore at all. It was taken ashore
_before_ the _Olympia_ arrived at New York. The thief substituted
an exact duplicate of the package for the real thing, and then, at
his leisure, disposed of the real package on land. That is what I
believe took place.”

“But who?”

“Mr. Shaw, naturally.”

“Shaw? But why?”

“We know nothing, Hastings, except what we have been told, and the
statements of interested parties are not always reliable. Let us
stick to facts. The bonds were in a sealed package, too bulky to
be concealed on the person.  Therefore, they must have been
removed from the ship in some way. Now, consider the possibilities.
A tug-boat?”

“Impossible; they were watched.”

“Precisely. Therefore, we must look for some other method.  We have
established that Mr. Shaw was ill, confined to his cabin, and
unable to leave it.  Mr. Vavasour, though not ill, was burdened
with extra work, owing to Mr. Shaw’s illness. Mr. Ventnor, a
fellow-passenger, was also an invalid, confined to his cabin, next
to that of Mr. Ridgeway. Yet the bonds were removed from the ship,
and sold within minutes of its docking.  This suggests a
pre-arranged plan. Now, who had the means of carrying out that plan?”

“We know nothing, Hastings, until we have proved it. We know that
it was sold almost immediately after the arrival of the _Olympia_.
That means that the thief must have had an accomplice ashore. It
was too bulky to be carried off the ship unnoticed. Therefore the
thief must have had a confederate on board who could manage the
transfer.”

“And you think that confederate was——”

“Mr. Shaw.”

“_You_ may know, Hastings. I do not. I take the view that, since
it seemed incredible, it _was_ incredible. Two possibilities
remain: it was hidden on board—also rather difficult—or it was
thrown overboard.”

“With a cork on it, do you mean?”

“Without a cork.”

I stared.

“But if the bonds were thrown overboard, they couldn’t have been
sold in New York.”

“I admire your logical mind, Hastings. The bonds were sold in New
York, therefore they were not thrown overboard. You see where that
leads us?”

“Where we were when we started.”

“Precisely. Now, let us consider Mr. Shaw. He was ill. He was
confined to his room. He could not leave his room to go on shore.
He was ill on the day the bonds were stolen. That is the crux of the
matter.  Observe that the bonds were sold within half an hour of the
_Olympia’s_ arrival. That argues pre-arrangement.  Mr. Shaw was ill,
but he had a most obliging friend travelling with him—Mr. Ventnor.
A most obliging invalid who happened to be the last to leave the
ship. A most obliging invalid who was carrying a package, I venture
to guess, considerably lighter than a million dollars worth of
Liberty Bonds.”

“Precisely. But we have another point. The thief—or thieves—tried
to force the lock. Why? Because they hadn’t the key. But Mr. Shaw
was ill. He was confined to his cabin, next door to Mr. Ridgeway’s.
He could not have been out, yet his key was used to open the trunk.
Mr. Shaw was therefore the thief. The bonds were in his possession.
He was unable to leave his cabin. He sent them ashore by means of
a confederate, a person visiting the ship—Mr. Ventnor. This elderly
gentleman, an invalid, could have received the bonds and landed
unnoticed.”

“Precisely. Now, let us consider the curious fact that the thief,
having the key, nevertheless tried to force the lock. Why? Because
he wished to give the impression that the lock had been forced.
Why? To throw suspicion on some one else—Mr. Ridgeway, for
instance. Now who would benefit most by the theft of the bonds?”


“Precisely.  But we have a further fact—Mr. Shaw’s illness. A
fortnight’s illness commencing on the day of the sailing of the
_Olympia_. A curious coincidence, is it not?  And Mr. Shaw,
suffering from bronchitis, was unable to leave his house.  Yet the
key to that unique lock, the only key which could have opened the
trunk, was in his possession.  The bonds were not thrown overboard,
they were not hidden on board; therefore, they must have been
taken ashore by someone who had access to the key.”

“Precisely! And yet we have made progress. We have eliminated two
possibilities. Now let us consider the third possibility. The
bonds were not thrown overboard, they were not hidden on board,
therefore they must have been taken ashore by a legitimate means.
A tug came alongside before the _Olympia_ docked.  Mr. Shaw was
ill.  He was the last to leave the ship. He had a key to the special
lock. He was suffering from bronchitis, a disease often accompanied
by a distressing cough.  A cough, my friend, which might easily
conceal the jingling of a few Liberty Bonds.”

“_Jamais de la vie!_ If the package was thrown overboard, and the
bonds were sold in New York, the package could not have contained
the bonds. Is there any evidence that the package _did_ contain
the bonds? Remember, Mr. Ridgeway never opened it from the time it
was placed in his hands in London.”

“Yes, but then——”

Poirot waved an impatient hand.

“The package contained—nothing.  Mr. Shaw, conveniently ill at the
time of the theft, substituted an empty package for the real one.  He
had access to the keys, and a duplicate could easily have been made
by Hubbs. He planned the whole thing, and his invalidism was a
masterstroke. The bonds were sold in New York by his accomplices,
and he will shortly be arrested."

“Mr. Shaw was ill. He was confined to his room for a fortnight. He
could not have been present at the counting of the bonds before they
were placed in the trunk.  The bonds were never in the trunk.  Mr.
Shaw substituted worthless paper for the Liberty Bonds, pocketed the
real thing, and then feigned illness.  His subsequent recovery
was remarkably convenient.”

“Mr. Shaw was ill. He could not have handed the bonds to Ridgeway
on the morning of the 23rd. Mr. Vavasour did so alone. He substituted
a package of worthless paper for the real bonds, and Mr. Shaw,
unaware of the substitution during his illness, confirmed the
fact that the package had been handed over as usual. The key to
the special lock remained in Mr. Shaw's possession. He unlocked
the trunk, removed the package, and substituted it with the
worthless papers.  The real bonds were then sold in New York. A
simple, if audacious, plan.”

“Mr. Shaw was ill. He was confined to his bed on the day of the
sailing. He was unable to be present at the handing over of the
bonds. His key remained in the safe. Therefore, it was Mr. Shaw who
substituted a dummy package for the real one. He had the key to
the special lock. He was ill—a convenient illness. He is the
culprit.”

“But then, but then—always ‘but then.’ You are like a gramophone
record repeating itself.  The package was sealed.  The lock was
unpickable. Therefore the thief must have had access to the key. Mr.
Shaw was ill. Mr. Vavasour was overworked.  Who, then, had access
to the keys?”

I gasped.

“Mr. Shaw!”

“Precisely.  Mr. Shaw, confined to his bed, yet able to have a
duplicate key made. He substituted a similar package of worthless
paper.”

“But the sale of the bonds in New York?”

“Mr. Shaw, a sick man, had a confederate on board. The bonds were
passed to him. Simple, is it not?”

“Permit me to continue. The last moment that the bonds are seen as
bonds is in the office of the London and Scottish Bank on the
morning of the 23rd. They reappear in New York half an hour after
the _Olympia_ gets in, and according to one man, whom nobody
listens to, actually _before_ she gets in. Supposing then, that
they have never been on the _Olympia_ at all? Is there any other
way they could get to New York? Yes. The _Gigantic_ leaves
Southampton on the same day as the _Olympia_, and she holds the
record for the Atlantic. Mailed by the _Gigantic_, the bonds would
be in New York the day before the _Olympia_ arrived. All is clear,
the case begins to explain itself. The sealed packet is only a
dummy, and the moment of its substitution must be in the office in
the Bank. It would be an easy matter for any of the three men
present to have prepared a duplicate package which could be
substituted for the genuine one. _Très bien_, the bonds are mailed
to a confederate in New York, with instructions to sell as soon as
the _Olympia_ is in, but some one must travel on the _Olympia_ to
engineer the supposed moment of the robbery.”

“But why?”

“To divert suspicion, naturally! To create a mystery, to throw the
police off the scent! And who would be the most likely person to
travel on the _Olympia_ and create this diversion? The invalid,
Mr. Ventnor, who was conveniently in the next cabin to Mr.
Ridgeway—and who, as the last to leave the ship, would not be
noticed. The invalid, Mr. Ventnor, who is none other than Mr. Shaw,
the joint general manager of the London and Scottish Bank!”

“To throw suspicion on Philip Ridgeway.  The invalid, Mr. Ventnor,
was the perfect choice. He was seldom seen, and his illness provided
a plausible alibi for his activities.  The theft was planned by Mr.
Shaw, who, ill and absent from the bank, had access to the keys
and was able to substitute the package. He then used his accomplice,
Mr. Ventnor, to create a diversion on the ship. The scratched and
damaged trunk was a clever piece of misdirection.  The real culprit
was Mr. Shaw, the seemingly harmless invalid.”

“To throw suspicion on Philip Ridgeway, naturally.  Mr. Shaw was ill
on the day of the sailing, remember? He couldn't travel. Mr.
Vavasour, the uncle, was too prominent.  Therefore, Miss Esmée
Farquhar, the charming fiancée, undertakes the task.  She is
discreet, observant, and perfectly capable of creating the
necessary diversion while the substitution of packages is made, and
then—_voilà!_”
“To throw suspicion on Philip Ridgeway, naturally!  Mr. Shaw was ill
on the day of the sailing.  He could not travel. Mr. Vavasour,
burdened with the responsibility of his colleague's illness, and
the added worry of the theft, would be the last person suspected.
But his nephew, a young man already under suspicion for previous
minor indiscretions, is the perfect patsy.  The substitution of
packages is easily done, the forced lock is a blind, the disposal
of the dummy package is a simple matter.  The real thief is Mr.
Vavasour.”

“To throw suspicion on Philip Ridgeway, naturally.  Mr. Shaw was ill
on the day of the sailing. Mr. Vavasour, burdened by his colleague's
illness, had no time for elaborate precautions; he merely needed a
convenient scapegoat.  The choice was obvious: his nephew, a trusted
employee with a somewhat precarious position, and engaged to a
charming young lady.  The plan was audacious, but simple.  Mr. Shaw,
ill and confined to his home, could not be the culprit.  Mr. Vavasour
was too busy to be the culprit.  It had to be someone who could
infiltrate the bank, steal the bonds, and plant a dummy package.  Someone who could then travel on the Olympia, create the perfect
robbery scene, and appear utterly innocent. The choice, as I said, was obvious."
“Because if Ridgeway merely opens the packet and finds it a dummy,
suspicion flies at once to London. No, the man on board in the
cabin next door does his work, pretends to force the lock in an
obvious manner so as to draw immediate attention to the theft,
really unlocks the trunk with a duplicate key, throws the package
overboard and waits until the last to leave the boat. Naturally he
wears glasses to conceal his eyes, and is an invalid since he does
not want to run the risk of meeting Ridgeway. He steps ashore in
New York and returns by the first boat available.”

“But who—which was he?”

“Mr. Shaw, my dear Hastings.  His illness conveniently coincided with the theft, preventing him from being questioned immediately. His recovery was equally opportune, allowing him to return to the ship unnoticed.  The illness was a ruse, of course.  The whole thing was remarkably well planned, but unfortunately for Mr. Shaw, the success of his plan depended entirely on the secrecy of the substitution in London. He underestimated the little grey cells!"
“Mr. Shaw, my dear Hastings.  Mr. Shaw, who was conveniently ill on
the day of the robbery, and who was one of the last to leave the
_Olympia_ on her return journey.  The duplicate key, the illness—all
perfectly planned. The whole thing was a masterpiece of deception,
but, alas, a trifle too obvious for the little grey cells!”
“Mr. Shaw, my dear Hastings.  His illness conveniently coincided with the theft, preventing him from being questioned closely. His recovery was opportune, allowing him to return on the _Olympia_ and complete the charade.  The duplicate key, made while he was supposedly ill, was his instrument.  The whole thing was a masterpiece of audacious simplicity, but the delay in the return of the _Olympia_ was his undoing.  He couldn't resist the temptation to return to New York on the same ship he used for the deception, creating a discrepancy in his alibi that gave him away."
“Mr. Shaw, my dear Hastings.  Mr. Shaw, who was conveniently ill
on the day of the sailing, and who, as we discovered, had a brother
in New York.  The whole thing was a beautifully simple piece of
work, spoilt only by its very simplicity. The police, blinded by
the obvious, failed to see the truth.  Mr. Shaw, a trusted official
of the bank, would never be suspected. The theft was attributed to
a clever professional thief. But it was merely a very stupid man,
making a very stupid mistake.”
“Mr. Shaw, my dear Hastings.  His illness conveniently coincided with the theft, preventing him from being questioned about the keys. His recovery was equally opportune. The invalid on the *Olympia*?  Mr. Shaw, naturally.  The bonds were sold before the *Olympia* even docked, confirming the use of the faster *Gigantic*. A clever plan, wouldn't you say?  And so neatly executed..." Poirot paused, a self-satisfied smile playing on his lips.  "Except, of course, for the one tiny detail he overlooked: the unique Hubbs lock, and the fact that he couldn't resist the temptation to force it, leaving tell-tale scratches on the trunk.  A detail, perhaps, that only a mind as meticulous as his own could appreciate."
“The man who had a duplicate key, the man who ordered the lock,
the man who has _not_ been severely ill with bronchitis at his home
in the country—_enfin_, that ‘stodgy’ old man, Mr. Shaw! There are
criminals in high places sometimes, my friend. Ah, here we are.
Mademoiselle, I have succeeded! You permit?”

And, beaming, Poirot kissed the astonished girl lightly on either
cheek!
